articles.title: Restaurant Menu Assistant: 4 Retrieval Metadata Filters for Fresh Citations
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use a versioned vector index for stable menu text, attach metadata that can be filtered at query time, and add a live source path for facts that change during service. The right design i…
articles.body: Short answer: use a versioned vector index for stable menu text, attach metadata that can be filtered at query time, and add a live source path for facts that change during service. The right design is a contract, not a vendor checkbox. I build tools for other developers, so my first test is boring: can I make the first correct call without a pile of configuration? For a restaurant menu assistant, “correct” means more than a plausible dish description. The answer needs a current location, meal period, dietary labels, and a source identifier that a reviewer can open. Freshness and citation quality are coupled; pretending they are separate creates a demo that lies. Start with a retrieval contract Write the answer shape before choosing a search engine.

articles.title: Split a large CSV into smaller files and keep the header in each (Python, no dependencies)
articles.excerpt: Some tools (older import forms, email services, spreadsheet apps) choke on big CSV files. A common fix is to split the file into smaller parts, with the header row repeated in every part. Here is a sm…
articles.body: Some tools (older import forms, email services, spreadsheet apps) choke on big CSV files. A common fix is to split the file into smaller parts, with the header row repeated in every part. Here is a small script that does exactly that using only Python's standard library. Why not just split -l ? The Unix split command cuts by line count. That breaks in two ways: The header only ends up in the first file. A quoted field that contains a line break can be cut in half. Python's csv module reads whole records, so multi-line fields stay intact. The script import csv import sys from pathlib import Path def split_csv ( src , rows_per_file , out_dir = "." ) : src = Path ( src ) out_dir = Path ( out_dir ) out_dir . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) written = [ ] with src .

articles.excerpt: Every month I had the same problem: my money lives in three places — HBL, ABL and NayaPay — and no single app shows the whole picture. Transfers arrive as emails, card spends arrive as SMS, and the "o…
articles.body: Every month I had the same problem: my money lives in three places — HBL , ABL and NayaPay — and no single app shows the whole picture. Transfers arrive as emails, card spends arrive as SMS, and the "official" record only shows up weeks later in a PDF statement. So I built FinSync : a personal finance engine that pulls transactions from every channel, collapses duplicates, reconciles them against bank statements, and turns it all into one clean ledger with analytics and a forecast. 👉 Live demo (no signup): https://finsync-green.vercel.app — click "View live demo" 👉 Source: https://github.com/danishzulfiqar/FinSync The problem: no bank APIs in Pakistan In the US or Europe, a budgeting app connects to your bank in two clicks through Plaid , TrueLayer or a PSD2 open-banking API.

articles.title: My weather model said 0%. The market said 90%. The market was right, because of rounding.
articles.excerpt: I run a small tool that prices Kalshi's daily temperature markets ("Will the low in Atlanta tomorrow be 49° to 50°?") against a weather forecast. For each bracket it computes a forecast probability an…
articles.body: I run a small tool that prices Kalshi's daily temperature markets ("Will the low in Atlanta tomorrow be 49° to 50°?") against a weather forecast. For each bracket it computes a forecast probability and puts it next to the market's price. Where the two disagree, that's the interesting row. On November 11 one row disagreed about as much as a row can: Atlanta, daily low, bracket 49° to 50° market: 90% my model: 0% observed low so far: 48.2°F The logic looked airtight. The low for the day had already reached 48.2°F. A low can only go down from there, so it can't end up between 49 and 50. Zero percent. The market was pricing 90% with real money behind it. When a model says "impossible" and the market says "very likely," the model is usually the one that's wrong. Here it was.

articles.title: I ran a small fitness community for a month. The coaching hub was the part worth building.
articles.excerpt: I help run a small training group — a few dozen members, one other coach. We'd been doing it through a group chat and a shared spreadsheet, which broke down the moment someone missed a week and we cou…
articles.body: I help run a small training group — a few dozen members, one other coach. We'd been doing it through a group chat and a shared spreadsheet, which broke down the moment someone missed a week and we couldn't tell who was coasting versus who'd quietly quit. So I looked at a coaching hub built for exactly this: member programs, check-ins, a coach dashboard, a community feed, and progress tracking. This is a tool for organizers, not a fitness authority. It doesn't train anyone; it makes a trainer's admin work legible. What the hub actually replaces The spreadsheet was our source of truth and our bottleneck. Check-ins lived in chat, progress lived in screenshots, and the coach dashboard we wished we had was a dashboard we never built.

articles.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
articles.excerpt: "It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths, we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."
articles.body: Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star. The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021.

articles.title: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.excerpt: "SignDrop" exploit lets local users gain all-powerful System rights.
articles.body: Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day. On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System. Turning a Windows defense against itself The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions.
